I read “Mr. Collins was not a sensible man, and the deficiency of nature had been but little assisted by education or society” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator says Mr. Collins was not sensible, and his lack of sense had not been helped by education or company. Next, craft. I notice the blunt judgment dressed in formal, balanced phrasing. The strongest word is “deficiency”: it means a lack, a clinical word that sums him up. Then, effect. How does the narrator judge Mr. Collins? My answer: Austen's narrator openly mocks Collins, explaining his mix of servility and self-importance; the description prepares us to laugh at him and to see why Elizabeth must refuse him.
